Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' For a severe mugging-related PTSD profile, markedly fragmented recall and very easy verbal access to the trauma narrative are hard to reconcile as describing the same current memory presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally incoherent for a severe mugging/robbery PTSD presentation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests low avoidance and relatively integrated, verbally accessible trauma memory, whereas simultaneously endorsing very vivid detailed recall and body-based painful reliving implies a highly sensory, distressing, poorly integrated trauma memory. This combination is possible in milder cases, but here it is hard to reconcile clinically within the same Memory profile. The Negative Appraisals items are coherent for robbery trauma, but the Memory selections do not fit cleanly with that node pattern or with the strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory linkage in the formulation.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: This item is more characteristic of ongoing threat/safety behavior than of a pure negative appraisal. In this profile, Threat is not endorsed and all Threat-related edges are inactive, while the active formulation is specifically centered on a Memory ↔ Negative Appraisals loop. The mistrust items fit robbery-related appraisals, but 'Constant Vigilance' introduces a prominent current-threat theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette: Arjun had been walking home from the downtown office where he worked the night shift, his hands wrapped around a thermos against the November chill. The streetlights had flickered out three blocks from his building, leaving him in the narrow stretch of shadow between a boarded-up bakery and a pharmacy. A figure stepped out from behind a dumpster, moving too fast to see clearly until it was close. The man’s voice was a low demand for his wallet. When Arjun fumbled with his jacket zipper, the attacker’s boot caught him hard in the ribs, driving the air from his lungs and sending a sharp ache into his lower back that would never truly leave. He handed over the money without a word, but the silence of the encounter and the sudden violence left him unable to piece together a coherent account of the night. He knew what had happened, yet when he tried to explain it to his wife, Maya, the sentences dissolved into unspeakable confusion, leaving him to stare at his hands while the memory of the strike burned behind his eyes. In the weeks that followed, the night of the mugging refused to fade. Instead, it settled into his body like a bruise that would not heal. Because he had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place and that people could not be trusted, Arjun found himself constantly scanning rooms for exits, judging every stranger by the set of their jaw. This quiet distrust began to dictate his days, and the moment his attention latched onto a suspicious gesture or an unfamiliar face, the vivid memory of the attack would surface with startling clarity. The recollection arrived in full, unbroken detail: the exact angle of the lamplight, the smell of wet asphalt, the precise weight of the boot against his side. That physical pain returned in waves, radiating through his ribs and spine exactly where the strike had landed, pulling his body back into the moment before he could consciously stop it. Now, six months later, Arjun spent his days moving through the hollowed-out offices of a corporate building, wiping down desks and emptying trash bins long after the staff had gone home. The silence there should have been peaceful, but it only amplified his hyperawareness. When a janitorial cart rattled against a doorframe or a coworker’s footsteps echoed from an upper floor, his breath hitched, and the vivid memory of the mugging surfaced instantly. As that memory took hold, the familiar pain flared in his ribs, and the recollection itself cemented his conviction that people were not what they seemed and that the world remained fundamentally dangerous. Each time the memory reinforced his negative appraisal, his body braced for the next threat, which in turn made the memories sharper, more insistent, and more likely to surface at the slightest provocation. The cycle had woven itself into his routine: he avoided working the east wing of the building where the lighting was poor, skipped weekend outings with Maya when she suggested walking through the downtown plaza, and began checking every bag he carried twice before leaving his apartment. The strain had begun to pull him away from his wife. Maya noticed how he flinched when she reached for his arm, how he stopped answering her questions about his day because the words kept slipping away, leaving him to sit in tense silence. He told himself it was necessary, that keeping his distance was the only way to stay safe, but the exhaustion was mounting. What finally brought him through the clinic’s glass doors last Tuesday was the morning he had dropped a heavy box of linens on his foot, twisted his ankle, and found himself unable to stand for nearly ten minutes, convinced someone was approaching to take everything from him again. He sat on the edge of the treatment couch now, his hands resting on his knees, his ribs still aching with the ghost of that old strike. He did not know how to untangle the knot of fear that had taken root in his chest, but he was desperate for it to loosen. He hoped, quietly and fiercely, that someone might help him understand why the past felt so present, and how he might ever walk through a room without bracing for a blow that had already ended.
